Supermarkets sell a wide range of everyday goods — groceries, packaged food, household items and personal care products — usually in several pack sizes and from many brands. Traditionally, customers visit the store, select items physically and pay at a billing counter. Behind the counter, the store purchases goods from suppliers, records stock, monitors shelf availability and reorders items that are running low.

Many small and medium stores still perform these activities with manual registers, standalone billing software or spreadsheets. Such methods are adequate for walk-in trade but provide no channel for customers who prefer to order from home, and they make it difficult to keep an accurate, up-to-date picture of stock across hundreds of items.

Business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce allows a retailer to publish its catalogue on the web and accept orders online. For a supermarket, an e-commerce system must go beyond a simple product list: products exist in multiple variants (for example 500 g and 1 kg packs), each variant has its own price and stock, items must be hidden when they are not meant to be sold online, and orders must be fulfilled from actual stock. The online storefront and the store’s back-office therefore have to share the same catalogue and inventory data.

The motivation for SmartCart is to provide a single, integrated system in which the store’s administrative data — catalogue, suppliers, purchases and stock — directly drives what customers see and can order online. Instead of maintaining the online catalogue separately from inventory, SmartCart uses one database so that a purchase entry increases available stock, an order reduces it, and a cancelled order restores it.

A supermarket that relies on walk-in trade and manual or disconnected record-keeping faces the following problems:
Customers cannot view the product range, prices or availability without visiting the store.
There is no channel for customers to place orders remotely and track their status.
Stock is recorded manually or in separate files, so the quantity available for sale is often inaccurate.
Purchases from suppliers are not linked to the stock available for sale.
Products with several pack sizes and prices are difficult to manage consistently.
Access to administrative functions is not controlled per employee or per task.
Order processing (confirmation, dispatch, delivery, cancellation) is not recorded in a structured way.
The problem addressed by this project is therefore:

to design and develop a web-based system that lets a single supermarket publish its catalogue online, accept and process customer orders, and manage catalogue, purchases and stock from a secure, role-controlled administration panel using one consistent database.

The need for SmartCart arises from the gap between the store’s internal operations and its customers’ expectations. An integrated system is needed so that (i) the online catalogue reflects the actual catalogue and stock, (ii) orders are validated against available stock before they are accepted, (iii) employees work through defined permissions, and (iv) every order passes through a clear set of statuses. A database-centred design with business rules enforced close to the data was required to keep stock and orders consistent.

2.5 Challenges Faced by Small Retail Businesses

Small retailers typically have limited budgets and technical staff. They need a system that is simple for employees to use, runs on commonly available infrastructure, and does not require separate products for the online shop and the back-office. They also need flexibility: not every item is suitable for online sale, and prices and pack sizes change frequently. At the same time, they must protect customer data and prevent unauthorised changes to prices and stock.

SmartCart addresses these challenges by combining storefront and administration in one application, by providing per-product and per-SKU online visibility, and by enforcing permissions for every administrative action.

The proposed system, SmartCart, is a web-based application that serves both customers and employees of a single supermarket. The storefront lets customers find products, choose a SKU, add it to the cart and place an order. The admin panel lets employees maintain all master data and process orders. Business rules that protect stock and order integrity are implemented in stored procedures so that they apply regardless of which screen triggers them.

In the design phase the overall architecture (single ASP.NET Core MVC application with storefront and admin areas), the module structure, the data flows and the use cases were defined. Decisions made in this phase include keeping customers and employees as separate identities, maintaining stock at SKU level, and enforcing order rules in stored procedures.

Development proceeded module by module. For each module the database objects were created first, then the repository and interface, then the controller actions and finally the views and scripts. Services and repositories are registered through a dependency-injection extension method called from Program.cs.

The storefront pages (Home, Shop, Cart, Wishlist, Checkout, Orders, Account) were built with Razor views and custom CSS, with JavaScript for listing, filtering and cart interactions. CHAPTER 12: SECURITY, LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE SCOPE
Customers and employees authenticate separately against the Users and AdminUsers tables. Passwords are hashed with the ASP.NET Core Identity password hasher and are never stored in plain text.

Employee authorisation is role-based: roles map to permission codes grouped by module, and admin actions declare [RequirePermission("Module.Action")]. Permissions are re-read from the database on the request, so client-side button hiding is not relied upon.

Input models use DataAnnotations; stored procedures validate business inputs such as address, phone and pincode formats, quantities and status transitions. Uploads are limited to jpg/jpeg/png/webp images up to 2 MB and one mp4/webm product video up to 20 MB.
Database access uses parameterised stored-procedure calls through Dapper and parameterised queries generated by EF Core; user input is not concatenated into SQL statements.
JWTs are signed and validated for issuer and audience, and are stored in separate cookies for customers and employees. Database trace logging masks password and token parameters.

AdminAuthMiddleware protects all /admin and /api/admin paths; customer-only features require a logged-in customer; customers can access only their own cart, wishlist and orders. GlobalExceptionMiddleware prevents unhandled errors from exposing internal details [verify production behaviour].
